1:
When the psalm was written divides them widely. John Calvin reads it as David’s at his accession, written by one who did not rashly rush forward and take forcible possession of a kingdom but was appointed to it, and who calls all the children of Abraham to ponder that grace. Adam Clarke thinks David most probably the author, though many think it written after the captivity, since it partakes of his spirit and everywhere shows the hand of a master. Keil and Delitzsch answer that it is without any doubt a post-exilic song, complain that one critic sweeps everything into vague generality, and name three occasions after the Exile that might have given it birth, the first being the keeping of the feast in the seventh month of the first year of the Return, when only a plain altar had yet been raised. The Calvin text carries a later hand as well, which observes that the psalm is without any title, so that its author is uncertain, and canvasses the return from captivity, an anointing at Hebron, the reign of Hezekiah and the age of the Maccabees, one authority declining to decide between them and preferring to note that the psalm was read at a solemn procession to the temple.

Whether it is a dialogue, and who speaks the parts, is a second question, and Adam Clarke reports two elaborate answers before rejecting both. One scholar joins this psalm to the one before it and divides the whole into four parts, giving the long middle section to the Messiah. A bishop goes further and makes the whole a triumphal processional song whose scene passes at the front gate of the temple: a conqueror with his train appears before it and demands admittance to give thanks for a dangerous expedition, and the verses are parcelled out among single voices, the conqueror alone, his train in chorus, and the priests and Levites within, the temple being taken as a type of heaven, the priests within as the angelic host, the conqueror as the Messiah and his train as the redeemed. Ingenious as both are, Clarke says, they seem to him too mechanical, and he prefers his own simple distribution of the psalm into parts.

The three summoned groups are read narrowly by one and widely by the rest. Adam Clarke takes the house of Aaron historically, as showing that the priesthood is still preserved and the temple worship restored. John Gill denies the literal restriction at every point: not the Israel brought out of Egypt only but the whole Israel of God, Jews and Gentiles; not the sons of Aaron literally, at least not only, since that priesthood is changed and all believers are now priests; and not the proselytes only but all who fear the Lord among any people. Matthew Henry reaches the same end more briefly, holding that the thanksgivings of all who truly fear the Lord are as pleasing to him as those of either house. Augustine of Hippo collapses the three into two and then into one, since both houses are among those that fear the Lord, and they are the little and the great. He also dwells on the shortness of the reason given: the praise of God could not be expressed in fewer words than that he is good, and he sees nothing more solemn than that brevity, recalling the answer given to one who called the Master good, that there is none good but God. C.H. Spurgeon presses the same point on the reader, that those who praise God only because he does them good should rise to a higher note and thank him because he is good; and he observes that grateful hearts are greedy of other men’s tongues and would monopolise them all for God’s glory.
5:
Whether these verses are the psalmist’s own or assembled out of older psalms is the quiet disagreement of the entry. Charles Ellicott calls the sixth verse a reminiscence of one earlier psalm and the seventh made up of another, and refers the reader there. The rest expound them as immediate experience. John Gill names three occasions when the distress might have been felt, when the man was encompassed by his pursuer, when he was at a foreign court, and when his own people talked of stoning him, and adds a fourth in the garden if the words are referred to the Messiah. Adam Clarke makes the speaker a standing proof and living witness of God’s mercy who bids others take encouragement from him. C.H. Spurgeon observes that the man had called upon the Lord when he was not in distress and therefore found it natural and easy to call upon him when he was.

The opening verse is rendered closely by two of them. Charles Ellicott would give it as out of the straitness I cried, and was answered with freedom, taking the sense of the last word from the parallel in an earlier psalm, and setting beside it a line from a play in which a soul is said at last to have elbow-room. C.H. Spurgeon notes that some read the original as a narrow gorge, so that the man passed out of the defile of distress into the well-watered plain of delight; and he adds that where God is concerned hearing means answering, since God is never himself shut up or straitened. John Gill and Adam Clarke both render the following verse as saying that the Lord is among the psalmist’s helpers, Gill drawing from it that he is the principal helper, one for all, standing in the room and stead of the rest, and Clarke that with God on his side he does not fear to look the whole company of his enemies in the face.

What the better trust is set against divides them at the close. Charles Ellicott takes the contrast politically: the word for trust is the one constantly used of the security an Israelite found in his relation to God, and the meaning here is apparently that fidelity to the covenant is better than alliance with foreign princes, though the larger sense in which the words apply to all men may of course be read into them. Adam Clarke reads it as a judgment on character, since men of high estate are generally proud, vainglorious, self-confident and rash, and often cannot deliver and will not when they can. John Gill takes the two verses as the conclusion drawn from everything before them, that those who trust in the Lord enjoy peace, are in safety, shall want no good thing and shall never be ashamed.
10:
The bees draw out the widest reading in the chapter. Adam Clarke finds in this verse and the next clause two of the finest images in Homer, the swarms pouring from a rocky cleft and darkening the coast, and the fire running through a mountain grove, and quotes both at length in an English poet’s version; the gleam of arms likened to fire, he says, is common to both writers, but the notion of that fire being quenched when the army is conquered is peculiar to the psalmist. Charles Ellicott works on the text instead. The image may be derived from a passage in the law, but the old Greek suggests that the poet used an original and far more expressive figure, since it reads that they surrounded him as bees surround the comb; possibly the word for comb dropped out of the Hebrew because the copyist was thinking of that passage in the law. He adds that the point of the second comparison is the rapidity with which a fire of thorns burns, which the old versions gave more plainly, and that a dramatist may have had the verse in mind who wrote of shallow jesters and rash brushwood wit, soon kindled and soon burnt. John Gill reads the figure from natural history, that bees in great numbers will attack and kill even horses, that besieged places have been delivered by throwing hives among the besiegers, and that in striking they lose their sting and quickly die.

Who the nations are, and what is done to them, is less settled than it looks. Adam Clarke reports that some refer the verse to the beginning of the reign, when the neighbouring peoples tried to keep the king from establishing himself, and others to the peoples who tried to prevent the rebuilding of the city and temple after the return. He then sets out five renderings of the verb that follows, from four scholars and three versions: that the psalmist will disappoint them, will cut them to pieces, has repelled them, will cut them off, or is avenged on them. John Gill takes the nations of the surrounding peoples in the psalmist’s own day, and then extends them to the enemies gathered against Christ, to the world set against the church at its first setting up, and to the last battles named in prophecy. John Wesley keeps to the neighbouring nations, stirred up by their defeats, by jealousy of a growing greatness and by hatred of the true religion. Charles Ellicott only makes the refrain more emphatic, that it is in the name of the Lord that this is done.

The sudden singular in the thirteenth verse is read three ways. John Gill takes it as an apostrophe to one particular enemy, naming the pursuer who cast a javelin at the psalmist, and the betrayer, and the adversary who thrust at Christ through others. Charles Ellicott renders it that thou didst thrust and thrust at me, and calls the sudden change of person and the challenge flung at the foes themselves very dramatic. John Wesley flattens it, holding that the singular word is here put collectively for all his enemies. Adam Clarke observes only that though the man possessed skill, courage and strength, these could not have prevailed had God not helped him, and that he gives God the glory of the victory; and John Gill makes the same point of the verse following, that having obtained help he ascribes nothing to himself.
15:
Whether the gates are doors or a person is the sharpest division here. Charles Ellicott holds that the next verse explains them as the gate of the temple, where the righteous alone entered, and that there does not seem the least reason for taking the words in any but this literal sense, though doubtless they are capable of endless spiritual applications; we must imagine, he says, a procession chanting its triumphal song and summoning the gates to open at its approach. John Gill refuses exactly that: the gate meant is not the door of the sanctuary, as the paraphrase has it, but the Messiah himself, the way of access to God and the door into the sheepfold, by whom alone righteous persons enter. John Wesley agrees that the place has a farther prospect than the psalmist and relates to an ascension and the opening of the gates of a blessed temple for himself and for all believers. Matthew Henry reports the same reading and adds his own use of it, that those who would enter into communion with God must become humble suitors for admission, and that our business within those gates is to praise. Adam Clarke keeps the scene dramatic and takes the following verse for the answer of the Levites to the king’s request. C.H. Spurgeon notes that a gate can stand for a seat of empire, as one famous title does, and calls the temple entrance the true seat of empire and, better, the gate of righteousness.

Who claims not to die is disputed on the same lines. Charles Ellicott says it is Israel and not an individual who claims a continuance of life for the display of God’s glory, while granting, as so often, that the hope is expressed to suit not only the community for whom the psalm was sung but each member of it. John Gill takes it personally and carefully, since the psalmist knew he must die and means only that his present afflictions would not issue in death; and then he refers the words to Christ, who came into the world to die and yet knew he should not die before his time nor remain long under death’s power. Adam Clarke keeps it shortest, that a man nigh unto death has been preserved to publish the wondrous works of the Lord. On the chastening that follows John Gill distinguishes the correction of a father, which all the afflictions of God’s people are, from a chastisement that was a proper punishment for sin, laid upon a surety.

Two smaller readings run against the grain. Charles Ellicott observes of the tabernacles of the righteous that whether we see in them an actual encampment, as the context seems to indicate, or take tents poetically for dwellings, depends entirely on the view taken of the date and occasion of the psalm — so that the question of when it was written comes back inside a single word. He also reads the exalted right hand as the attitude of a warrior, the hand lifted up to strike, where John Gill takes it for a power made eminent and conspicuous, Adam Clarke for a hand that performed prodigies, and John Wesley for a power that appeared evidently and wrought gloriously. Matthew Henry closes the passage by pointing forward, calling what follows an illustrious prophecy of the humiliation and exaltation of our Lord, and observing that when an apostle applied it directly to the chief priests and scribes none of them could charge him with misapplying it.
22:
Who the rejected stone is turns on a reading nobody else notices. Charles Ellicott points out that there is no article in the Hebrew, so that it is a stone rather than the stone, and identifies it without hesitation: Israel is this stone, counted of no account in the political plans of those who were trying to shape the destinies of the eastern nations at their own pleasure, yet destined in the purpose of God for a chief place in the building up of history; the image is afterwards developed by a prophet and, with the messianic hope poured into it, prepared for the use of Christ himself and for the apostles who repeatedly applied it to him. John Gill reaches the opposite conclusion by elimination, rejecting in turn the reading that makes the stone a governor of the return, the reading of two Jewish commentators that makes it the people of Israel, and the paraphrase that makes it the psalmist. John Wesley keeps both terms of the figure, since the commonwealth and the church are compared to a building in which the people are the stones and the princes the builders, and just as those master-builders rejected the king, their successors rejected Christ, to whom the words agree more properly. C.H. Spurgeon reads it first of the king raised into office by divine decree and then of Christ, and explains the rejection: the builders could see no excellence in him that they should build upon him, he could not be made to fit their ideal of a national church, and he was a stone of another quarry than themselves. Adam Clarke declines to expound the two verses here at all and refers the reader to his notes on the gospel where they are quoted.

What day is meant is answered as broadly or as narrowly as each has read the psalm. Charles Ellicott offers either the festival for which the psalm was composed, perhaps the feast of tabernacles, or more generally the day of the triumph God had won. Adam Clarke keeps it to the occasion in hand, that the Lord having called him to triumph this is the day appointed for it, a gracious opportunity to be improved to God’s glory. John Wesley makes it a season sanctified never to be forgotten. John Gill multiplies the possibilities, the day of the entry into the city, or of the resurrection, or the day kept in commemoration of it, or rather the whole gospel dispensation made bright by the sun of righteousness. Of the verse between them Charles Ellicott says only that this change of destiny, which made Israel of sudden political importance, is to be ascribed to none but God himself, where John Gill takes the same words of the choosing and laying of the stone, of the permission under which it was rejected, and of the exaltation that followed.
25:
The cry that opens the entry is traced to its liturgical use by all of them. Adam Clarke notes that the words were sung at the feast of tabernacles while green branches were carried, and that from them comes the word the children used at the entry into the city. John Gill says the same and adds that the cry was first a wish of health to a king, used when the tribes united to make him king over all the people. Charles Ellicott corrects only the grammar, that the second word is not the adverb of time, so that the sense is save, we pray. John Wesley assigns the sentence to the Levites. The welcome that follows is taken by all four as an antiphon: Adam Clarke calls it the answer of the Levites to the king, John Wesley the words of the priests appointed to bless in God’s name, and Charles Ellicott the greeting of the Levite in charge to a procession approaching the gates, adding from rabbinical writings that pilgrim caravans were welcomed on their arrival at the city in just these words. John Gill keeps to the multitude that used them at the entry.

What light was shown divides the literal from the figurative. Charles Ellicott says the choice is difficult: taken literally the clause may repeat the earlier verse about the day, or, if the feast of tabernacles is particularly in view, may connect with the pillar of cloud and fire which that feast very probably commemorated, a suggestion he calls most worthy of notice; taken figuratively it would mean the light of salvation and hope; and there may also be an allusion to the priestly benediction, where the same verb stands. Adam Clarke goes further than any of them toward the literal, suggesting that at this moment a divine splendour perhaps shone upon the whole procession as a proof of God’s approbation. John Gill takes the light of the coming of the Messiah and of the gospel shining into the heart, and John Wesley of dark clouds scattered and a people set in peace and safety.

What is to be bound at the horns of the altar is the hardest clause of the psalm. Adam Clarke gives the paraphrase which makes a prophet command that the little one be bound with chains for a solemn sacrifice until it is offered and its blood sprinkled on the horns; he adds that the word may mean the festival victim, and that several instead translate it as keeping the festival with thick boughs up to the horns of the altar, which is how the old Latin and Greek understood the passage. John Wesley takes the plain sacrificial sense and supposes the horns to have been made for this very use, that the beasts should be bound and killed there. Charles Ellicott denies that the plain sense will work at all, since the Hebrew says as far as to rather than to, and no satisfactory account can be given of binding a victim in that way. C.H. Spurgeon closes on the doubled confession of the next verse, calling the repetition a double determination and turning it into a resolve that however others may blaspheme and however dull he may feel himself, as long as he has any being that being shall be spent in praise; and he observes that the psalm concludes as it began, making a complete circle of joyful adoration. Adam Clarke says the same of the last verse, that it is the general doxology in which all join.
